name: Genoa Blue
lede: Genoa Blue is a muted greenish blue in Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary; the name points to Genoa, the port whose cloth gave the world the word jeans.

sections.title: Genoa, cloth and dye
sections.body:
Pastoureau traces the word *jean* to the Italo-English *genoese*, meaning from Genoa [1]. Cloths of the Genoa family, first wool and linen and later linen and cotton, were used from the sixteenth century for boat sails and sailors' trousers [1]. Levi Strauss's trousers were called jeans by the years 1853 to 1855, and when denim replaced the canvas about ten years later the name stayed [1].

St Clair offers a different route: the word is believed to come from *bleu de Gênes*, or Genoa blue, which she describes as a cheap indigo dye favored for sailors' uniforms [2]. Books disagree on emphasis: Pastoureau gives a cloth, St Clair a dye, and only St Clair uses the color name [1][2].

sections.title: Swatch and cloth
sections.body: The swatch here comes from Maerz and Paul's dictionary of 1930, as cited by the ISCC-NBS in 1955 [3]. It is a greenish blue, nearest to moderate greenish blue by 4.6 units of ΔE2000, and lighter and greener than dark work cloth such as [[denim]] [3]. See also [[indigo]] and [[teal]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This tone appears in 66 paintings in our archive, 0.28 per cent, as photographed [4]. Paul Cézanne has it in 5 of 50 paintings [4]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is not a pigment test [4].
